data.title: 3 ‘Strong Buy’ Data Center Stocks to Bank on for 60%+ Upside
data.description:
Data centers remain critical to AI’s rise despite worries about stricter regulation. This article looks at data center-related names that analysts rate a Strong Buy. They are: Sterling Infrastructure (STRL), Viavi Solutions (VIAV), and EnerSys (ENS). According to TipRanks’ Compare Top Data Center Stocks tool, the stocks offer at least 60% upside.

These stocks are for investors seeking exposure to companies that help power the industry’s physical infrastructure. Sterling Infrastructure leads the group with about 121% upside based on the average price target of $645.

Sterling Infrastructure (STRL)

Sterling is a Texas-based construction company. It helps data center and semiconductor companies to develop their sites. This includes helping to build the electrical systems for such sites.

Beyond data centers, it also provides design and construction services to clients in sectors such as aviation, ports, and public transportation.

Sterling’s shares are down about 2% year-to-date. Analysts expect the stock to rally by about 121% over the next 12 months. This is based on the average price target of $645.

Viavi Solutions (VIAV)

Viavi is an Arizona-based network testing equipment company. The firm makes hardware and software that tests fiber-optic cables for data center connections. Examples include testing chassis and fiber microscopes.

The U.S. company also makes optical coatings. These are ultra-thin microscopic layers applied to materials. These coatings help control light for purposes like preventing counterfeit money and enabling 3D facial recognition.

Viavi’s shares have surged by about 83% since the start of the year. Still, analysts see room for another 79% rally over the next 12 months. This is based on the average price target of $55.

EnerSys (ENS)

EnerSys is an industrial stored energy company. The Pennsylvania-based firm builds heavy-duty battery systems and chargers. These serve as backup power infrastructure for data centers. Clients also deploy these products for warehousing, cell towers, space infrastructure, and military equipment.

The company’s shares have risen by less than 1% year-to-date. However, analysts expect ENS stock to rise by about 69% over the next 12 months. This is based on an average price target of $241.67.

data.title: Has Nvidia Bottomed? Consider This First
data.description:
According to reports circulating Friday morning, former Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang had a third extramarital affair. This is in addition to previously disclosed affairs with alleged spy Alice Huang and with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s Vice President of Healthcare. 

I’m not a moralist. I believe extramarital affairs are a private matter between those parties directly impacted. It’s none of my business. However, Nvidia isn’t a marriage. It’s a business. Many of our readers invest in the stock, and that makes it my business. If you own or are considering owning shares of Nvidia, you are taking partial ownership of an entity that was shaped by Mr. Huang. 

Time to Buy?

I keep getting the question: Is now the time to buy? Nvidia shares seem to have bottomed, at least for now. With Mr. Huang’s exit, shares are up in Friday morning pre-market trading. The stock traded in the low $170’s, after finding support earlier this week.

Nvidia Shares Bounce Back

In fact, Nvidia shares are becoming more attractive, at least from a technical standpoint. The stock appears to have formed a bullish double-bottom pattern (points A and B). Thursday’s selloff occurred on the stock’s highest volume in over a year (arrow).

At this point, it would be easy to say that the bad news is out, the sellers are washed out, and the stock has bottomed. Despite these positive technical developments, I’m not a buyer of Nvidia at this time.

Fool Me Once…

We know that Mr. Huang is a cheater. This leads to some difficult questions.

If Mr. Huang was willing to cheat in a marriage, would he also cheat in business? If he was willing to deceive his wife, would he also be willing to deceive his shareholders?

When Nvidia reports earnings Tuesday after the closing bell, will you trust that those figures are 100% accurate? Or will you be shocked if, at some point in the future, Nvidia’s earnings or revenues need to be retroactively adjusted?

How would that affect Nvidia’s stock price?

Spy Games

Regarding Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged spy Alice Huang, can we say with 100% certainty that he never suspected she might be an operative for a foreign government? U.S. intelligence agencies suspected as much for the past year, and circulated a memo to that effect among U.S. policymakers in the spring of this year.

Aside from Mr. Huang, are there others remaining within Nvidia who were fooled by Ms. Huang? Will you be surprised if it comes out later that she had accomplices within Nvidia?

What effect would those revelations have on the stock price?

Bottom Line

These are not accusations. These are fair questions that need to be answered before I’m once again willing to put money to work in Nvidia.

I believe the sensational headlines are obscuring the real risks in this situation. Some folks assume that because Jensen Huang is gone from Nvidia, his actions can no longer have a negative effect on the stock’s price.

That’s a dangerous assumption. There are plenty of other options on the table.

Now is an excellent time to join TheStreet Pro. Click here. 

This article is being shared as premium content from TheStreet Pro. It was written by Ed Ponsi.

data.title: AMD vs. Marvell: One AI Stock Won the Rebound, the Other Is the Buy, Says Investor
data.description:
The AI trade has had a bumpy time of it lately. Chip stocks sold off after the midterms on worries that the results could slow the AI buildout, and Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) and Marvell (NASDAQ:MRVL) were caught up in it. Both have bounced back since, but not by the same amount.

AMD, which builds the processors that run AI workloads, has led the recovery, aided by a record quarter and benefiting from the upheaval at Nvidia, where Jensen Huang resigned as CEO yesterday, following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. Marvell, which supplies the custom chips and connections that move data between them, has bounced but is still weighed down by its plan to buy optical specialist Lumentum in an all-stock deal valued at $115 billion, and its shares sit almost 50% below their June record.

Investor Robert Izquierdo, who contributes to The Motley Fool, has compared the two to decide which one deserves a place in a portfolio heading into 2027.

The investor has no complaints about AMD’s business. Third-quarter revenue climbed 45% year over year to a record $13.4 billion. Data center sales, now close to two-thirds of the total, jumped 97% to $8.5 billion. That was driven by demand for EPYC server processors and the launch of AMD’s Instinct MI450 GPUs. Management expects growth to speed up from here. It is guiding for roughly $17 billion in fourth-quarter revenue, which would be a 66% YoY increase at the midpoint.

AMD’s customer list keeps getting longer. The company already has a multiyear agreement to supply OpenAI with MI450 accelerators. In late October, it said its Helios rack-scale systems were installed and being tested at Meta. This week, it disclosed plans to invest $2.5 billion in Anthropic stock. That’s part of a commitment of up to $5 billion, tied to Anthropic deploying AMD chips.

The problem, as Izquierdo sees it, is that success comes at a price. AMD’s string of AI wins, plus money moving away from Nvidia, has pushed its shares to a rich valuation. AMD trades at approximately 39x forward earnings, above its five-year average of 35x. Meanwhile, Marvell trades at roughly 29x forward earnings following its recent selloff.

Marvell’s numbers are also impressive. Fiscal second-quarter revenue rose 37% YoY to a record $2.74 billion, led by 46% growth in data center sales. Management expects revenue of roughly $12 billion for fiscal 2027, about 45% higher than last year. This month, the company said third-quarter revenue is in line with the $3.15 billion midpoint of its guidance.

The bigger news came at Marvell’s October 6 investor day. The company raised its fiscal 2028 target (the year ending January 2028) to about $20 billion from $18 billion, ahead of what Wall Street had expected. It also set a fiscal 2031 goal of $70 billion to $90 billion. CEO Matt Murphy added that Marvell’s AI addressable market could reach $400 billion by 2030.

Izquierdo notes that those targets came before the Lumentum deal. Lumentum’s revenue jumped 137% YoY to $1.26 billion in the quarter ended September 26, and it expects $1.575 billion to $1.625 billion in the December quarter. Under the deal terms, Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each share they own. In his view, adding the laser and optics maker gives Marvell another strong source of growth for years to come.

Neither stock is free of risk. AMD competes with Nvidia and Intel, relies on a handful of manufacturing partners, and faces export limits on advanced AI chips. Those limits have already led to inventory charges. Marvell depends on a small group of big customers and on Asian foundries, which exposes it to geopolitical tension and natural disasters in the region. It could also lose business as cloud giants design more of their own chips.

The Lumentum deal adds its own uncertainty. Because it’s paid in stock, existing Marvell shareholders will own about 67% of the combined company. The deal still needs shareholder and regulatory approval and isn’t expected to close until the first half of 2028.

Still, Izquierdo sees Marvell’s lower valuation and the extra growth Lumentum could bring as the stronger combination. He would buy Marvell over AMD going into 2027. (To watch Izquierdo’s track record, click here)

On the Street, both these stocks are rated Strong Buys, although one is seen as now having far more upside. AMD’s average price target stands at $652.18, a figure making room for 12-month returns of 11.5%. MRVL’s average target lands at $323.63, suggesting the stock will gain 97% in the year ahead. (See AMD stock forecast or MRVL stock forecast)

data.title: 3 Vanguard ETFs with ‘Strong Buy’ Ratings and 30%+ Upside Potential for 2027
data.description:
Vanguard ETFs have long been popular among investors looking for affordable exposure to a wide range of stocks. With diversified portfolios spanning various sectors and investment strategies, these funds offer an accessible way to participate in the stock market. But with so many options available, how can investors determine which ones offer the greatest potential?

One approach is to examine Wall Street analysts’ ratings and price targets for the stocks held within each fund. With 2027 approaching, we used the TipRanks Best Vanguard ETFs tool to pick three ETFs that currently carry Strong Buy consensus ratings, with each offering at least 30% upside potential based on analysts’ forecasts.

Vanguard Growth ETF (VUG)

For investors who believe the biggest names on Wall Street still have room to grow, the Vanguard Growth ETF offers a way to own many of them through a single investment. The fund tracks the Morningstar US Large Cap Growth Index, which focuses on large U.S. companies with strong growth characteristics. With an annual expense ratio of just 0.03%, investors pay only $3 per year for every $10,000 invested.

VUG currently holds 136 stocks, with total assets of $217.62 billion. Its portfolio leans heavily toward technology, led by Nvidia (NVDA), which accounts for 13.49% of assets, followed by Apple (AAPL) at 12.51%, Microsoft (MSFT) at 9.75%, and Alphabet Class A (GOOGL) at 5.16%. Together, these four companies account for more than 40% of the fund.

Turning to Wall Street, VUG earns a Strong Buy consensus rating on TipRanks, based on 125 Buys and 9 Holds among 134 of its underlying holdings. The average analyst price target of $110.50 implies about 31% upside from current levels. (See VUG forecast)

Vanguard Mega Cap Growth ETF (MGK)

Want to concentrate on the companies that dominate the U.S. stock market? The Vanguard Mega Cap Growth ETF takes that approach by tracking the Morningstar US Mega Cap Growth Index, which invests in some of the largest growth-oriented companies in the country. Its annual expense ratio of 0.05% means investors pay $5 for every $10,000 invested, making it a relatively inexpensive way to gain exposure to corporate giants.

Unlike funds that spread their investments across hundreds of companies, MGK maintains a relatively concentrated portfolio of just 53 holdings, representing $32.27 billion in total assets. Nvidia leads the way with a 13.72% weighting, followed closely by Apple at 12.55%. Microsoft accounts for another 9.48%, while Alphabet Class A represents 4.99%. These four stocks alone make up more than 40% of the portfolio, leaving the ETF particularly sensitive to the performance of the largest tech names.

Despite that concentration, analysts remain bullish on MGK’s prospects. The ETF carries a Strong Buy consensus rating, with 50 Buys and only 2 Holds among 52 of its underlying holdings. The average price target stands at $113.90, suggesting ~33% upside potential from its latest price of $85.78. (See MGK forecast)

Vanguard S&P 500 Growth ETF (VOOG)

Not every company in the S&P 500 has the same growth prospects, and the Vanguard S&P 500 Growth ETF is designed to focus on those with stronger growth characteristics. Rather than investing in the entire benchmark, the fund tracks the S&P 500 Growth Index, which selects companies based on factors such as earnings growth, sales growth, and price momentum. Investors also benefit from a modest annual expense ratio of 0.07%.

The ETF offers broader exposure than MGK, holding 153 stocks with total assets of $26.13 billion. Nevertheless, tech remains a central part of its portfolio. Nvidia is the largest holding at 15%, followed by Microsoft at 10.34%, Apple at 6.60%, and Alphabet Class A at 5.48%. That combination gives investors considerable exposure to AI and cloud computing, alongside other growth-oriented companies across the U.S. market.

Wall Street also sees considerable room for gains. VOOG has earned a Strong Buy consensus, supported by 145 Buys and 6 Holds among 151 of its underlying holdings. The average analyst price target of $106.10 points to 33% upside potential from current levels. (See VOOG forecast)

data.title: Nvidia Stock Just Lost Something It Can’t Buy Back, Says Top Investor
data.description:
For more than three decades, Wall Street treated Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Jensen Huang as the same thing. That ended on Thursday. Huang stepped down as president, CEO and board member with immediate effect. It came after reports linked him to a relationship with a Megaspeed executive who U.S. intelligence believes was working for Beijing, and then to a second relationship with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Hours after he quit, Reuters reported a third relationship, with a different Nvidia employee who hasn’t been named.

CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO, and Harvey Jones has become the board’s first-ever chair. The board says it will look at both internal and external candidates for the permanent job. Washington isn’t finished with Huang either. Three House committees want him to give closed-door testimony on December 1 or face subpoenas. The shares fell as much as 14% on Thursday, then recovered to close down about 4%. The stock is down again in Friday’s session and now sits remains 33% below its October 6 record.

5-star investor Stone Fox Capital (SFC) thinks Nvidia’s shareholders are unlikely to be better off without the man who made it the world’s most valuable company. Huang owns only about 3.5% of the stock, so he had no real way to overrule the board.

History doesn’t offer much comfort, in SFC’s view. When big tech companies replace a dominant leader, the results are mixed. Microsoft’s shares went nowhere for years under Steve Ballmer, while Apple thrived under Tim Cook after Steve Jobs. Intel is the closer warning. It once had a commanding lead in chips, then lost ground to Nvidia and AMD while it went through several CEOs. The investor puts Nvidia’s chances of finding a successor who takes it higher at about a coin flip and expects a year or more of uncertainty. Prediction markets have CUDA creator Ian Buck as the front-runner, and an insider would at least keep things steady.

For SFC, the big unknown is whether Huang played any part in the alleged flow of chips to China. The Information linked Alice Huang’s network to at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia shipments to Chinese firms. China denies the spy claims, and nothing public shows that Huang knowingly helped Beijing.

The business itself still looks solid. Nvidia reports fiscal third-quarter results on November 17, and Wall Street expects revenue of about $109 billion, up roughly 91% year over year. SFC argues that supply limits Nvidia’s sales more than demand does, so another buyer would quickly take any orders a customer pulls. Fourth-quarter guidance matters more, since the scandal broke only days into that period. The stock trades at roughly 10.5x analysts’ fiscal 2028 EPS estimates, and its P/E has dropped to a 14-year low.

The danger is execution. Google and AMD are pushing harder into AI chips. SFC worries that without a strong leader, Nvidia could lose the pricing power behind its large share of industry revenue. The investor also expects earnings estimates to come down as customers press for discounts.

Bottom line, while SFC stays an NVDA bull, the investor has downgraded his NVDA rating from Strong Buy to Buy. (To watch Stone Fox Capital’s track record, click here)

On the Street, NVDA stock now has a Moderate Buy consensus view, a rating based on 27 Buys vs. 11 Holds. At $247.58, the average price target implies shares will gain 55% in the months ahead. (See Nvidia stock forecast)

data.title: Micron vs. Sandisk: Both AI Stocks Look Dirt Cheap, but This Top Investor Says One Has More Staying Power
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) and Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) spent the first half of 2026 hogging the top of the market’s leaderboard, carried by an AI build-out that has been using up memory chips faster than factories can produce them.

Since late June, though, both have been sliding hard. Doubts about how long AI spending can keep up its pace, and then a chip sell-off after the midterm elections, have wiped out a big piece of those gains.

On a year-to-date basis, however, the numbers still look strong. Micron is up about 140% in 2026, but it trades around 38% below its late-June peak. Sandisk has had a more meteoric rise and a rougher decline. It soared by roughly 880% between the start of the year and late June, but has since fallen by ~63%, though it still holds a gain of 211% for the year.

So, where to now for these high-flyers? 5-star investor Geoffrey Seiler, who contributes to The Motley Fool, believes the AI memory boom has room for both companies, but he thinks one of them is better set up.

Seiler notes that the two companies work in different parts of the memory market. DRAM is the fast, temporary memory that processors use as a scratchpad, and it loses everything once the power goes off. NAND flash keeps data without power. It’s slower but far cheaper, and it ends up in SSDs and memory cards. Micron makes both. Among the three companies that dominate DRAM, it is the smallest, yet it still holds nearly a quarter of that market, according to TrendForce, along with a mid-teens share of NAND. In its fiscal fourth quarter, DRAM made up 73% of Micron’s revenue and NAND 26%. Sandisk, by contrast, is a NAND-only business with roughly 11% of the flash market, according to Counterpoint Research.

What links the two markets right now is high bandwidth memory, or HBM. This is a specialized type of DRAM packaged right next to GPUs and other AI accelerators so those pricey chips aren’t left waiting on data. Seiler notes that HBM demand tracks accelerator demand, while production is lagging. Part of the reason, he explains, is that HBM relies on the same extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography tools used for advanced logic chips. Only ASML makes those machines, so new capacity comes online slowly and chipmakers compete for it. He adds that HBM needs roughly three times the wafer capacity of standard DRAM, and adding cleanroom space takes several years.

Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron have steered so much of their production toward HBM that supply of everyday DRAM and NAND has tightened, which has pushed prices up across the board. Seiler points out that ordinary memory prices have risen faster than HBM pricing, and that has been a big driver of growth at both companies. NAND is getting an extra lift from AI labs that store their training data on large SSD arrays.

Memory has a long history of booms followed by busts, but Seiler argues that AI gives this cycle a lasting source of demand. Both companies have been signing longer-term supply deals. In September, Micron said its customer agreements cover an estimated 35% or more of its revenue through 2030.

Despite all this, both stocks look cheap, trading at roughly 4x forward earnings.

Seiler separates the two on market structure. DRAM is a much more concentrated market than NAND, and HBM is central to the AI build-out. “I think that Micron is the clear stock of the two to buy if you were only going to buy one, as I expect the current memory supercycle to last longer for DRAM,” Seiler summed up. (To watch Seiler’s track record, click here)

As for Wall Street’s take, the analyst consensus sees both as Strong Buys, with plenty of upside projected. Micron’s average price target lands at $1,624, implying the shares will gain 116% over the coming months. SNDK is expected to add 148%, considering its average target clocks in at $2,112. (See MU stock forecast or SNDK stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Until Liftoff,’ Says Investor About Rocket Lab Stock
data.description:
Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) has a full order book for a rocket that hasn’t left the ground. The space company’s third-quarter earnings report on Monday showed record sales and a wave of new contracts. The Pentagon also gave Neutron, Rocket Lab’s next-generation rocket, a public vote of confidence. The catch is that the vehicle the long-term story depends on is still in testing.

Scanning the results, investor Bohdan Kucheriavyi sees plenty to like. Revenue jumped 73% year over year to $267.8 million, led by Space Systems, and management guided for up to $290 million in Q4.

What stands out most to the investor is demand for Neutron. Rocket Lab signed eight Neutron contracts worth more than $515 million, so the first 16 flights are booked and the next openings don’t come until the 2030s. It also raised the base price on several missions to $70 million from about $55 million. Kucheriavyi links this to a shortage of launch capacity, which could get worse as SpaceX winds down commercial Falcon 9 flights. On top of that, the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital announced a $150 million conditional loan commitment to help Neutron fly more often after its debut. With roughly $4.7 billion in cash and securities, the company has enough to finish the rocket and to fund its pending $8 billion takeover of satellite operator Iridium Communications, which it agreed to in June.

The trouble is that Neutron still hasn’t flown. Its debut slipped to 2027 after voids were found in the forward dome of the first-stage tank. Management won’t set a date until testing wraps up, likely in the first quarter. That pushes revenue further out: only about a third of the backlog is expected to turn into sales within 12 months, down from roughly 45% at the end of June.

The Iridium deal also needs FCC approval, and SpaceX, Ligado and Globalstar have raised concerns with the regulator. A long review could delay the deal’s mid-2027 close.

Dilution is another headwind. The share count has climbed from about 544 million at the start of the year to an expected 681 million basic shares in Q4, including preferred stock, and that’s before Iridium holders get their shares. Economists also expect the Fed to raise rates in December, which makes rich valuations harder to defend for companies that aren’t yet profitable. The competition isn’t waiting either. Neutron missed out on NASA’s Moon Base launch orders, and AST SpaceMobile plans to build its own rocket.

The stock trades at roughly 43x trailing 12-month sales, which is a steep price for a company that isn’t yet profitable. Kucheriavyi’s updated DCF model leans on Wall Street’s revenue forecasts for the next decade, and it assumes Neutron spending will keep Rocket Lab in the red through 2027. Even with those forecasts, the model shows only modest upside, and most of it depends on Neutron. Another delay could push forecasts lower. He would rather see Neutron fly first, and rates Rocket Lab stock a Hold (i.e., Neutral). (To watch Kucheriavyi’s track record, click here)

Three of the Street’s analysts agree with that take, but with an additional 15 Buys, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus view. At $95.35, the average price target implies shares will climb 57% higher over the coming months. (See RKLB stock forecast)

data.title: Down 60%, Is Nebius Stock Now a Buy? Top Investor Weighs In
data.description:
Nebius’ (NASDAQ:NBIS) third-quarter earnings report on Thursday was really two stories, and the market chose the gloomier one. The AI cloud provider beat Wall Street’s revenue and earnings forecasts and made real progress on profits. It also warned that delays at third-party data centers will move some of this year’s revenue into next year, and it handed shareholders a much bigger construction bill. The report landed while the AI infrastructure trade was still shaken by Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia, and the stock got hammered.

The stock fell about 17% on Thursday, and is continuing to fall today with the shares down by 9% as part of another tech rout.

Management now expects 2026 revenue at the low end of its $3 billion to $3.4 billion range. It also raised this year’s capex forecast to about $27 billion, up from a prior $20 billion to $25 billion. Nebius stock now sits 61% below its June high.

Investor Jonathan Weber, who ranks among the top 3% of investors on TipRanks, doesn’t blame the quarter for the selloff. He puts it down to general nerves about AI, possibly a sell-the-news reaction, and concern that Nvidia under new leadership may be less friendly to neoclouds like Nebius and CoreWeave than Huang was.

On the numbers, the investor is impressed. Revenue jumped 571% year over year to $980.8 million, helped by new data centers and better pricing per megawatt. Total operating costs fell to 95% of revenue from 189% a year earlier, which left Nebius with an operating profit. The GAAP net loss from continuing operations shrank to $37.5 million from $119.6 million, while CoreWeave’s net loss widened.

The 5-star investor is far less comfortable with what comes next. Growth like this came off a small base and won’t last. Interest costs are still keeping Nebius in the red at the GAAP level. Its adjusted profit looks better only because it leaves out share-based compensation, which comes at a real cost to shareholders through dilution.

Spending is the bigger worry. Nebius plans $40 billion to $45 billion in capex next year to chase its 2027 revenue target of $12 billion to $13 billion. Customer prepayments will cover part of it, but Weber expects a big jump in debt and more share issuance on top. The company is already burning cash fast, and he sees plenty of risk in the business model. He is also unsure how the relationship with Nvidia will change under its new CEO.

He doesn’t consider the valuation low either. Nebius trades at roughly 12x this year’s expected revenue, though at less than 3x its 2027 target, so much depends on the buildout arriving on schedule.

Bottom line, Weber remains on the NBIS sidelines, rating the stock a Hold (i.e., Neutral). (To watch Weber’s track record, click here)

On the Street, 2 analysts are also on the fence, and with an additional 9 Buys and 1 Sell, the stock claims a Moderate Buy consensus view. The average price target lands at $265.90, implying the shares will gain 131% in the months ahead. (See NBIS stock forecast)

data.title: Don’t Wait for the AI Bubble to Burst, Warns Investor on Nvidia Stock
data.description:
The selling in Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) shows no signs of letting up, with shares falling nearly 4% on Friday and extending their November losses to 22%. Just days ago, the AI chip giant was preparing for another blockbuster earnings report, but Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation has changed everything. With quarterly results due Tuesday, November 17, investors now have far more to worry about than revenue and profits.

Wall Street is also struggling to determine what Huang’s departure means for Nvidia’s future. Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon has downgraded the stock, citing uncertainty surrounding the leadership transition, while D.A. Davidson’s Gil Luria has warned that crucial decisions involving investments, acquisitions, and product development could face delays. CFO Colette Kress has assumed temporary control, although replacing such an influential founder presents challenges that extend far beyond filling an executive position.

Yet, investor Damir Tokic sees an even greater threat looming over the semiconductor powerhouse. He believes the upcoming financial results could expose weaknesses in the industry’s spending frenzy, potentially triggering a selloff that reaches far beyond Nvidia itself.

Tokic acknowledges the company’s outstanding earnings record, having exceeded earnings expectations in seven of the past eight quarters. Analysts currently anticipate revenue of $108.81 billion and earnings of $2.47 per share, representing annual growth of about 91% and 90%, respectively. However, the investor believes historical performance offers little reassurance about what happens next.

His primary concern involves spending projections for 2027, which previously anticipated industrywide AI investments reaching $1 trillion to $1.2 trillion. Following the Democrats’ midterm election victory, Tokic expects stricter regulations governing data-center construction to force corporations into reducing their expansion plans. That could leave Nvidia facing an unwelcome choice between lowering its longer-term outlook and withholding those forecasts altogether.

“In my opinion, this could signal the end of the AI trade,” Tokic warns.

Such an outcome, the investor argues, could undermine the financial arrangements supporting much of today’s infrastructure expansion. Nvidia has invested in companies that purchase its processors, creating interconnected relationships involving equity investments, financing arrangements, and equipment orders. Should capital expenditures weaken, these arrangements could unravel, threatening revenue expectations throughout the sector.

The former chief executive’s exit adds another concern, given his personal involvement in establishing those partnerships.

“In my opinion, Huang’s resignation is the first ‘domino’ to fall in the circular web of AI, and others will follow,” the investor argued.

Tokic therefore sees little reason to purchase Nvidia based on its valuation alone, despite its relatively low forward price-to-earnings multiple. Current profit estimates could prove overly generous if future chip demand falls short, leaving investors holding shares that only appear inexpensive.

For Tokic, the greatest danger lies in the possibility that tech companies are investing far more in computing infrastructure than their customers can financially justify. He points to a troubling historical parallel, warning that “Nvidia could end up like Cisco in the dot-com bubble burst aftermath.”

His warning also extends to the broader stock market, where tech leaders represent a significant portion of the S&P 500’s value. A collapse in AI investment could therefore trigger widespread equity losses while weakening economic activity enough to threaten a recession.

With those risks in mind, Tokic assigns NVDA stock a Sell rating, arguing that investors should leave before deteriorating expectations expose the full extent of the industry’s vulnerabilities. (See NVDA stock forecast)

data.title: 3 Strong-Buy Growth Stocks With Over 40% Upside, According to Analysts
data.description:
Growth stocks can offer strong return potential when their businesses continue to expand. Amphenol (APH), TSMC (TSM), and Rocket Lab (RKLB) stand out with Strong Buy ratings from analysts and more than 40% potential upside based on their average price targets.

Each company has a different growth driver. Amphenol is gaining from rising demand for AI data centers. TSMC is seeing strong demand for advanced chips. Rocket Lab is growing its launch and spacecraft business as more companies and governments invest in space. Their strong revenue growth and exposure to expanding markets make them worth watching.

Below are the details.

Amphenol (APH)

Amphenol makes connectors, cables, and sensors used in data centers. Rising demand for AI and data centers has boosted sales of its products, including fiber-optic components.

Amphenol has a strong track record of growth. In Q3 2026, revenue rose 65% year-over-year to $10.23 billion, while adjusted EPS increased 74% to $0.80. In 2025, its revenue rose 52%, while adjusted EPS grew over 70%.

Analysts have rated Amphenol stock as a Strong Buy, backed by 10 Buys and one Hold assigned in the last three months. APH’s average stock price target of $108.67 suggests a potential upside of over 40% from current levels.

Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM)

TSMC is the world’s leading advanced chipmaker, supplying major companies in the AI, smartphone, cloud, and auto markets. In Q3, revenue rose 17.6% sequentially in Taiwan dollars and 16.2% in U.S. dollar terms to $46.7 billion. The result came in above the high end of its guidance, driven by strong demand for advanced chips. Chips made using 7nm or smaller process technology accounted for 79% of total wafer revenue.

TSMC expects Q4 revenue of $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion. This would mark a 58% rise year-over-year at the midpoint. The company also raised its 2026 revenue growth outlook to around 44% in U.S. dollar terms.

TSM stock’s average price target of $563.75 implies an upside potential of 42%. TSMC stock has a Strong Buy rating based on nine Buys.

Rocket Lab (RKLB)

Rocket Lab is a space company that builds rockets and spacecraft and provides launch services. It is growing its launch and space systems business as demand from commercial and government customers increases. Q3 revenue reached a record $267.8 million, up 73% from a year earlier and 14.4% from the previous quarter. It also beat the company’s guidance range of $250 million to $265 million.

Rocket Lab expects revenue to reach nearly $1 billion in 2026, compared with just $35.2 million in 2020. It projects a GAAP gross margin of around 35% and a non-GAAP gross margin in the 40% range. This marks a major improvement in profitability as the business grows.

Analysts have rated RKLB stock as a Strong Buy, backed by 15 Buys and three Holds assigned in the last three months. Meanwhile, Rocket Lab’s average stock price target of $95.35 suggests a potential upside of 57.7% from current levels.

data.title: Oracle (ORCL) Faces a Cash Crunch, but Its AI Bet Still Looks Promising
data.description:
Oracle (ORCL) faces a cash crunch, but its artificial intelligence (AI) bet still looks promising. Best known for its database software, the company has become one of the biggest builders of AI data centers. Its capex is at a record high. Now the obvious question is whether Oracle can earn a decent return on it all.

I’m bullish on Oracle. Demand for its AI cloud keeps growing, and management has finally put a date on its cash problem. At today’s price, much of the bad news already looks priced in. However, it is not entirely a safe bet.

Oracle stock is down about 34% this year, even though revenue grew 30% last quarter and adjusted earnings beat estimates. The worry is that Oracle is spending far more cash than it brings in, and borrowing heavily to do it. However, I believe its latest moves show a realistic way out.

Oracle’s AI Demand Is Real

Oracle’s AI demand is real, and the latest quarter shows it. Its cloud infrastructure business, which rents out computing power, grew revenue 121% to $7.4 billion. Oracle also delivered 850 megawatts of new AI capacity to customers, almost triple the previous quarter’s. Its graphics processing units (GPUs), the chips that run AI models, were in use 97.9% of the time.

The detail I like most comes from renewals. GPUs whose contracts ended were renewed or resold at a 20% premium, even though most of them were at least four years old. That eases a common fear that AI hardware loses its value quickly.

More growth is already under contract. Oracle’s remaining performance obligations (RPO) reached $664 billion. RPO is the value of signed contracts that haven’t turned into revenue yet, and Oracle expects about half of it to become sales within 36 months.

Oracle Is Building on Borrowed Money

Oracle is building much of its AI business on borrowed money, and that is its biggest problem. Last quarter, capex hit $28.5 billion, more than Oracle’s entire revenue of $19.3 billion. That pushed free cash flow to -$5.4 billion. For the full fiscal year, management expects capex of $90 billion to $95 billion.

Oracle had about $125 billion of borrowings at the end of August, and its newest bonds pay 7% to 8.65% a year. On the plus side, Oracle’s debt-to-equity ratio, or what it owes for each dollar that belongs to shareholders, fell to 2.34 from 4.36 a year earlier. That decline came from share sales and profits, not from debt repayment, which remains high. In July, S&P (SPGI) cut Oracle’s credit rating to BBB-, one notch above junk.

This is where return on invested capital (ROIC) matters. It measures how much profit a company earns on all the money tied up in its business. Adding up TipRanks’ figures for the last four quarters, I get about 9%, down from about 11% a year earlier. Earning about 9% while paying more than 7% on new debt leaves a thin cushion. That worries me most.

Customers are the other risk. OpenAI, Oracle’s biggest customer, is still losing money. Microsoft (MSFT), meanwhile, is winding down a 2023 deal to rent AI capacity from Oracle, reportedly because the servers use older Nvidia (NVDA) chips that no longer meet its needs.

Oracle’s Cash Problem Looks Fixable

Oracle’s cash problem looks fixable to me, mainly because management finally has a plan. After its last quarterly report, management still wouldn’t say when free cash flow would turn positive. That changed at its Investor Day in October. Oracle now expects positive free cash flow in the second half of Fiscal 2028 and more than $30 billion in Fiscal 2029.

To me, that is a good signal. Investors’ biggest fear was that the spending had no end. Now there is a date and a number that management can be held to.

Oracle also capped new stock and bond sales through Fiscal 2030 at $20 billion and raised the full amount in early November, splitting it evenly between $10 billion in stock and $10 billion in bonds. If it sticks to that cap, it shouldn’t need more new money from investors.

New deals help, too. Last quarter, Oracle signed more than $30 billion of AI contracts that needed no extra cash from the company, mostly because customers paid upfront or brought their own hardware. I find that more reassuring than any long-term revenue target.

Is Oracle Stock a Bargain?

Oracle stock looks like a bargain to me, at least next to its own history. Its trailing-12-month (TTM) price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio is about 20x, meaning investors pay about $20 for each dollar of reported profit Oracle made over the past year. At the end of each of the last five fiscal years, its P/E was between about 29x and 42x. Microsoft, another heavy AI spender, trades at about 27x.

The forward P/E, based on analysts’ adjusted earnings estimates for the next 12 months, is about 15x. That is down from about 29x in late November 2025 and near its lowest since 2022. Analysts expect adjusted earnings per share (EPS) to grow almost 36% in Fiscal 2028. If so, about 15x looks cheap to me.

The main risk is execution. Oracle wants to more than triple its capacity by the end of Fiscal 2028, to about 10 gigawatts. If big data centers come online late, revenue and cash flow will arrive late, too.

How Does Wall Street See Oracle?

Wall Street is bullish on Oracle, with a Strong Buy consensus rating based on 28 Buys, four Holds, and one Sell assigned in the last three months. At $241.83, the average Oracle price target implies 90.26% upside potential.

Bernstein’s Mark Moerdler, a five-star analyst on TipRanks, reiterated his Buy rating and $325 price target on November 10, implying about 156% upside. He sees two catalysts: more clarity on OpenAI’s ability to pay for its computing commitments, and Oracle’s return to positive free cash flow. His target looks too high to me, but I agree that free cash flow will decide where the stock goes next.

The Bottom Line

I’m bullish on Oracle. It is a good business in a tough spot. I usually avoid companies with this much debt and such thin returns on capital. Oracle stands out because it has a huge backlog of signed contracts and, now, a target date for positive free cash flow. If management delivers, today’s price may look cheap in a few years.

data.title: SpaceX vs. Tesla: Which Elon Musk Stock Has More Upside, According to Analysts?
data.description:
Elon Musk‘s companies, SpaceX (SPCX) and Tesla (TSLA), are both down more than 11% year-to-date. However, Wall Street sees very different upside potential for the two stocks. According to TipRanks’ Stock Comparison Tool, SpaceX has a Strong Buy consensus rating, with 76% upside potential based on its average price target. Tesla, meanwhile, has a Moderate Buy rating, with its average price target pointing to just 3.6% upside.

Earlier this month, both stocks fell after Democrats won the U.S. midterm elections, defeating several candidates backed by Musk. The result raised concerns about tougher oversight of Musk’s businesses.

SpaceX Delivers a Strong Q3, While Tesla Falls Short

SpaceX reported a strong third quarter, with revenue jumping 161% year-over-year to $14.58 billion. Net profit reached $4.4 billion, well above the $1.8 billion forecast. Within segments, AI revenue surged more than ninefold to $7.6 billion, overtaking Starlink revenue. Connectivity revenue, which includes Starlink, grew 69% to $5.25 billion.

CFO Bret Johnsen also said Q1 2027 revenue could reach $33 billion to $37 billion, well above the $22.2 billion analyst estimate.

Tesla delivered a mixed quarter. Revenue came in at $28.05 billion, flat from a year ago and in line with estimates. Adjusted EPS of $0.50 beat the $0.45 forecast, but net income fell to $787 million and automotive revenue dropped 3%.

Tesla also lowered its 2026 capital spending forecast to about $20 billion from more than $25 billion, raising questions about the pace of its AI and robotics investments.

Latest Analysts’ Views on SPCX

Bank of America analyst Ronald Epstein added SpaceX to the firm’s US 1 List of top investment ideas and maintained a Buy rating with a $275 price target. He cited strong launch growth and better-than-expected Q3 results. Epstein believes SpaceX is on track to reach a $100 billion revenue run rate this year.

Epstein holds a five-star rating on TipRanks and ranks 212th among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by the platform. He has a 61% success rate.

Similarly, Stifel’s analyst Jonathan Siegmann also maintained a Buy rating on SPCX, with a $190 price target, implying an upside of 35%. He highlighted SpaceX’s position in orbital data center infrastructure. Siegmann sees potential delays in state-level approvals for land-based data centers as an opportunity for space-based computing and other alternative infrastructure.

Deutsche Bank analyst Edison Yu reiterated a Buy rating on SpaceX with a $250 price target. He views the stock’s recent pullback following the midterm elections as a buying opportunity. Yu believes local opposition and restrictions on traditional AI data centers could limit computing capacity, benefiting SpaceX’s cloud and orbital computing business.

Wall Street’s Views on Tesla

JPMorgan analyst Rajat Gupta maintained a Hold rating on Tesla with a $430 price target, implying 8% upside. He flagged potential hurdles in the reported Tesla-SpaceX merger talks. Gupta noted that SpaceX’s U.S. defense contracts and Tesla’s large presence in China could create regulatory and governance challenges.

Jefferies reduced its Tesla price target to $375 from $400. Analyst Philippe Houchois pointed to a gap between the stock’s valuation and its estimates. It also warned that robotaxi and humanoid robot projects could add to costs before they generate meaningful revenue.

Bank of America Securities analyst Alexander Perry, however, maintained a Buy rating and a $460 price target. He sees strength in Tesla’s core business and believes its autonomy business could become a major profit driver by the end of 2027. In Q3 2026, Tesla Auto business contributed 73% to the total revenue and almost 70% to the total gross profit.

SPCX or TSLA: Which Stock Offers Higher Upside, According to Analysts?

SpaceX has an average 12-month price target of $246.30, implying 76% upside. In comparison, Tesla’s average price target of $411.86 suggests 3.6% upside.

data.title: NVDA vs. AVGO: Which Stock Has More Upside, According to Analysts?
data.description:
Nvidia (NVDA) and Broadcom (AVGO) are two semiconductor stocks that could benefit from growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power, but one may offer more upside, according to analysts. For Nvidia, recent leadership changes have added a new layer of uncertainty. Long-time CEO Jensen Huang has resigned, and CFO Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO. This shake-up comes just as big technology companies are accelerating their data center spending, prompting investors to watch whether rivals like Broadcom can gain market share.

Nvidia focuses on AI accelerators and data-center graphics processing units (GPUs), while Broadcom provides AI networking chips, custom processors, and infrastructure software. We used the TipRanks Stock Comparison tool to compare both stocks, see which offers more upside, and review analysts’ ratings. The tool also lets users compare stocks by P/E ratios, dividend yields, Smart Scores, market cap, and other metrics.

Is NVDA a Buy, Sell, or Hold?

Nvidia designs GPUs, networking hardware, and proprietary software like Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) that power global AI infrastructure. Co-founder Jensen Huang led the chipmaker from its 1993 inception to a $5 trillion valuation, concluding a 33-year tenure as CEO on November 12, 2026. The company will report Q3 FY2027 earnings on November 17, and analysts estimate revenue of $108.72 billion and earnings per share (EPS) of $2.47. If it meets this forecast, revenue will increase 13% sequentially and almost 90% year-over-year. This will be the company’s first earnings report without Jensen at the helm.

On TipRanks, Nvidia has a Moderate Buy consensus, with several analysts downgrading the stock to Hold yesterday after the resignation announcement. Evercore ISI downgraded NVDA to In Line from Outperform with a price target of $186, down from $465. The firm believes that the probe into Jensen Huang’s case will take several months and expects the stock’s P/E multiple to continue to compress, with Nvidia’s lack of succession planning adding to the risk. The average NVDA stock price target of $254.84 implies a 53.34% upside from the last price of $166.19.

Is AVGO a Good Stock to Buy?

Broadcom designs the high-speed networking switches and custom AI chips (XPUs) that help hyperscalers like Alphabet (GOOGL), Meta (META), and OpenAI reduce their dependence on off-the-shelf GPUs. Led by CEO Hock Tan, Broadcom pairs its chip business with a software arm built around VMware, which brings subscription sales from corporate cloud and mainframe clients. The company is set to report Q4 2026 earnings on December 9. Analysts estimate revenue of $34.90 billion and EPS of $3.83.

Year-to-date, the stock is up 5.28%. Broadcom has a Strong Buy consensus, with 29 of the 31 analysts covering the stock rating it a Buy. The average price target of $519.50 suggests 42.58% upside from current price levels. Rothschild & Co Redburn downgraded AVGO to Hold from Buy with a price target of $398, down from $595 today. The firm cited financing concerns surrounding Broadcom’s major AI customers, OpenAI and Anthropic (ANT).

Conclusion

Nvidia currently offers more upside based on analyst price targets, but uncertainty around its CEO transition and upcoming earnings could change the picture. Broadcom may benefit if AI customers look to diversify their chip suppliers, though Nvidia’s strong technology position could limit any immediate shift.

data.title: UBS Urges Investors to Be More Selective on AI — and Recommends 2 Tech Giants to Buy
data.description:
The sudden departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has given AI investors something new to worry about. After more than three decades at the helm of the chip giant, Huang’s exit has raised concerns about the risks of relying too heavily on a single executive, particularly when that person’s leadership has been central to a company’s success. For an industry that has helped drive much of Wall Street’s gains in recent years, it’s another reminder that rapid growth doesn’t eliminate the need to consider what could go wrong.

And leadership uncertainty is hardly the only concern. Competition between the U.S. and China over AI technology continues to play out against strict restrictions on advanced semiconductor exports, with little indication that Washington will ease those rules anytime soon. As computing power becomes more important to national security, governments are also taking a closer look at where chips are manufactured, sold, and ultimately used, adding another complication for companies operating across international markets.

Taken together, these developments are changing how investors should approach the AI sector, at least according to the UBS Chief Investment Office (CIO).

“While we retain our conviction in the structural AI opportunity, we think these events reinforce the case for greater selectivity and diversification as the tech investment cycle evolves. We continue to favor financially strong hyperscalers; tighter future compute capacity could increase the value of existing infrastructure, while lower future capital spending could support free cash flow. Within AI ‘picks and shovels’ (semiconductors and hardware), we would stay selective and favor quality companies with less margin expansion to unwind, alongside defensive technology exposures such as payment networks and potential beneficiaries of lower memory costs within consumer electronics,” the CIO team wrote.

In other words, UBS still sees opportunities in AI, but it isn’t treating every company benefiting from the technology as an equally attractive investment. The bank has singled out two household names that fit its preferred approach, and Wall Street appears to agree, with both earning Strong Buy consensus ratings. Using the TipRanks database, we’ll examine why these two stocks have made the cut and how much upside analysts see from current levels.

Microsoft (MSFT)

We’ll start with Microsoft, the $3.9 trillion company that leads the world’s software industry. Microsoft is Wall Street’s third-largest publicly traded firm, behind only Apple and Nvidia, and is best known for its Windows and Office software packages. But while Windows and Office are the world’s premier business and personal computing software packages, Microsoft sees its future in AI and cloud computing.

The company can fairly claim that it was an early backer of AI, putting large investments into the technology well before the current boom even began. In 2019, Microsoft invested $1 billion in OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, and the companies have had a close relationship ever since. To date, Microsoft’s investment in OpenAI totals $13 billion, and the companies reworked their relationship earlier this year. Microsoft has a 20% revenue share deal with the AI developer, and OpenAI is not exclusively tied to using the Azure platform – although OpenAI is still making intensive use of Azure, both for development and distribution of AI technology.

The nature of the agreement does many things, for both companies, but for investors it acts to highlight just how important Azure, Microsoft’s cloud computing service, has become. Azure is easily one of Microsoft’s fastest growing products, and the software company has been regularly incorporating AI capabilities into it.

Last month, Microsoft released its fiscal 1Q27 results and showed better-than-expected results on both revenue and earnings. The company’s top line for the quarter came to $92.3 billion, up 19% year-over-year and beating the forecast by $1.54 billion. The $4.89 non-GAAP EPS came in 17 cents per share ahead of the estimates.

This top-tier stock has caught the attention of a top-tier analyst, UBS’s Karl Keirstead. The 5-star industry expert says of the world’s leading software firm: “Microsoft shares remain our top defensive idea, with Azure/other estimates moving higher and the stock trading at just 22x CY27E non-GAAP EPS. The Azure upside had a few sources, but one key one to call out was the strength of OpenAI in the quarter, which correlates to higher Azure growth via strong Astra AI model sales that get distributed via Azure. Given that OpenAI is now 30%+ of Azure revs (higher accounting for indirect sales), Azure growth could be more variable depending on large lab customer growth.”

For Keirstead, all of this adds up to a Buy rating, and his $700 price target implies a 34% upside for the coming year. (To watch Keirstead’s track record, click here)

That’s about right, compared to the Street consensus. MSFT’s 39 recent analyst ratings include 35 Buys and 4 Holds, to give the stock its Strong Buy consensus take. The stock is trading for $523 right now, and the 632.48 average price target suggests that MSFT will appreciate by 21% on the one-year time frame. (See MSFT stock forecast)

Amazon (AMZN)

The next stock we’ll look at is another of the trillion-dollar-plus mega-caps, Amazon. Amazon is the fifth-largest publicly traded company on Wall Street, and boasts a market cap of $2.9 trillion. Amazon has long been the world leader in online retail, and in the last twelve months it ran past Walmart as the world’s largest retail company.

Amazon’s total revenue in its last full fiscal year came to $716.9 billion, and while online retail still made up the largest share of that figure, at some $588 billion, the company is expanding its non-retail footprint – especially in AI. The company’s highest-profile business segments are AI-related, and more importantly, they are fast-growing and promise to push Amazon ever higher.

AWS, of course, is the place to start when we talk about Amazon’s growth components. The popular cloud service is expanding rapidly. While retail sales in the North American and International segments grew 6% and 5% respectively in Q3 of this year, AWS was up 39% in the quarter, to hit $46 billion. AWS powered its growth through the expanding set of AI tools and apps available on the cloud service, which are complementing the already-popular array of more traditional software offerings. A look at the last several quarterly reports shows just how quickly AWS has been accelerating in recent months. In 3Q25, that figure was up to 20.2%; in 4Q25, it was up 24%.

Of course, AWS is not the only place to look for Amazon’s AI exposure. The company has been moving into the silicon chip business, and its Trainium semiconductor chips, a custom-built AI accelerator family, are broadening the pool of products available for AI providers. Amazon has a commitment from OpenAI to use up to two gigawatts of Trainium chip capacity, and in addition, OpenAI will also expand its AWS contract by $100 billion over the next 8 years.

The big picture here shows that AI, in various forms, is the fastest growth factor for Amazon. In the 3Q26 report, the last released, Amazon’s total revenue came to $201.9 billion – a total that was up more than 12% year-over-year, although it missed expectations by nearly $340 million. As noted above, AWS accounted for $46 billion of that total, or just under 23%.

At the bottom line, Amazon generated an EPS of $1.89. This figure was down from $1.95 in the prior-year period, a decline that was attributed to pre-tax gains in 3Q25 from the company’s investments in Anthropic – an AI provider and the firm behind Claude.

For UBS’s Stephen Ju, the key point here is the strength of AWS and its potential to continue delivering growth. The analyst writes: “Amazon until now had typically eschewed from offering expectations or even acknowledge that AWS can accelerate, but mgm’t highlighted that: 1) AWS revenue growth is expected to exceed 40% in FY27 and FY28, and 2) it is positioned to become a $1T business over the next 5-10 years. The net big picture takeaway here is that over the course of the prior ~2 years during which AWS embarked on an accelerated pace of investment, it is on course to transform the business into something that has enough visibility to sustain over a five year period, what should be a doubled rate of growth vs the ~20% that investors were contemplating earlier this year. Further, the updated Performance Obligations disclosure of $578B suggests it onboarded close to $100B in new business.”

Ju’s stance backs up his Buy rating on Amazon, and his $352 price target implies a one-year upside potential of more ~32%. (To watch Ju’s track record, click here)

Overall, AMZN has picked up 43 recent analyst reviews, and their split of 42 Buys to 1 Hold gives This mega-cap tech giant its Strong Buy consensus rating. The stock is trading for $267.44 and its $324.90 average target price indicates room for a gain of 21% in the next 12 months. (See AMZN stock forecast)

data.title: ‘History May Repeat Itself’: Investor Warns Nvidia Stock Could Follow Intel’s Troubling Path
data.description:
Only 4.3%? That’s how much Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) stock lost on Thursday, despite the magnitude of Jensen Huang’s resignation earlier in the day. After all, his abrupt departure is arguably the biggest market story of 2026, overshadowing even SpaceX’s blockbuster IPO. The exit of the man who spent more than three decades building Nvidia into the world’s dominant AI chipmaker could have sent shares into a much deeper tailspin.

Zoom out a little, however, and the picture looks less reassuring, with Nvidia shares having lost 19% of their value since the beginning of November. And for investors wondering whether the damage could go much further, history offers a troubling comparison.

One investor, known by the pseudonym Envision Research, sees similarities between Nvidia’s current predicament and the sudden resignation of Intel CEO Brian Krzanich in June 2018, following revelations of a relationship with an employee that violated corporate policy.

Both chipmakers turned to their chief financial officers for temporary leadership, with Intel appointing Bob Swan and Nvidia handing the reins to Colette Kress. Neither corporation was facing an operational collapse when its chief executive departed, making the comparison worth examining.

Indeed, Intel had delivered a cumulative total return of 258% during Krzanich’s five-year tenure. Nevertheless, its price-to-earnings multiple eventually contracted from around 25 times to merely 10 times, while the shares needed about two years to regain their previous levels. Even after that recovery, the valuation remained well below its earlier peak.

For Envision Research, those figures offer a reason to approach Nvidia’s recent losses with caution.

“I don’t suggest investors to bottom fish here despite the large price correction,” the investor cautioned.

His concern is that the market may require an extended period to rebuild confidence in the chipmaker, regardless of its commanding industry position or healthy balance sheet. Intel’s experience suggests that strong underlying operations cannot necessarily prevent investors from assigning a lower earnings multiple for years.

But the comparison becomes more troubling when Envision Research examines what sets these two leadership crises apart.

Huang wasn’t simply another corporate executive overseeing an established enterprise. As Nvidia’s co-founder and chief architect of its technological direction, he helped determine everything from product development to competitive strategy. Envision Research believes replacing that combination of expertise, vision, and industry influence will be far harder than finding someone to succeed Krzanich.

There is also the nature of the controversy itself, with Nvidia facing national-security concerns and questions about potential export-control violations, while Intel’s episode concerned an internal workplace policy.

Still, the investor acknowledges that Nvidia retains formidable advantages, including its dominant position in AI accelerators and attractive earnings projections. With its forward P/E already down to around 18 times, the stock may look tempting to those seeking a bargain after the recent retreat. However, Envision Research remains unconvinced.

“With these considerations, I keep seeing a neutral risk/reward curve for NVDA despite attractive valuation ratios and growth projections,” the investor summed up.

data.title: CoreWeave or Palantir: Cathie Wood Buys $16M of One AI Stock, Sells $10M of the Other
data.description:
It’s been a wild couple of days for CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) investors. After surging nearly 25% on Wednesday following encouraging quarterly earnings, the neocloud stock reversed course on Thursday, falling nearly 7%. The pullback came as disappointing guidance from rival Nebius raised concerns about the cost of expanding AI infrastructure, while Nvidia’s leadership crisis following Jensen Huang’s departure added another reason for investors to retreat from the sector.

Meanwhile, Palantir (NASDAQ:PLTR) hasn’t had much luck escaping the recent tech selloff either. Shares of the AI software company have lost about 18% over the past month, despite delivering another quarter of strong revenue growth. With investors becoming less willing to pay premium valuations for AI stocks, even companies reporting strong results could find themselves on the losing side.

But Cathie Wood appears to have made up her mind about where she wants more exposure. On Thursday, the ARK Invest founder purchased 283,022 CoreWeave shares through her firm’s funds, worth about $16 million at current prices, while selling 58,339 Palantir shares, valued at $10 million. The transactions suggest Wood was willing to increase her exposure to AI infrastructure while reducing her position in one of the sector’s best-known software companies.

CoreWeave’s Earnings Give Investors Plenty to Consider

CoreWeave’s latest financial results offer some explanation for Wood’s buying decision. Third-quarter revenue climbed 168% year over year to $3.66 billion, while the company’s backlog reached $132.5 billion. Perhaps more importantly, CoreWeave raised its full-year revenue outlook to between $13 billion and $13.3 billion, reflecting continued demand for the computing capacity needed to train and operate AI models.

The company also expects to achieve positive adjusted net income during the first half of 2028. However, getting there won’t be cheap. CoreWeave anticipates spending between $37 billion and $39 billion on capital expenditures this year, leaving investors to weigh its expanding customer commitments against the enormous cost of delivering them.

Thursday’s slide also illustrated how sensitive the stock remains to developments elsewhere in the industry. Nebius warned of heavier capital spending and slower-than-anticipated revenue recognition, while Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia raised concerns about the future of the chipmaker’s financial support for CoreWeave. Nvidia is one of CoreWeave’s largest investors, supplies its GPUs, and has committed to purchasing billions of dollars worth of unused computing capacity. With CoreWeave carrying a heavy debt load, any reduction in Nvidia’s backing could make its expansion plans more challenging to finance.

Overall, if Wood is looking for upside in CoreWeave, Wall Street’s numbers offer some support for that view. The stock has earned a Moderate Buy consensus rating from analysts, with 21 Buys, 6 Holds, and 3 Sells issued during the past three months. The average 12-month price target of $105.63 implies ~87% upside from current levels. (See CRWV stock forecast)

Palantir’s Growth Isn’t Enough to Silence the Skeptics

Whatever investors think about Palantir’s valuation, there’s little denying the pace at which the company is growing. Revenue nearly doubled in the third quarter, reaching $2.31 billion, while management lifted its 2026 outlook to $8.53 billion. Perhaps the most revealing development was the company’s U.S. commercial revenue surpassing its government revenue for the first time.

Yet, investors found something to worry about beneath those numbers. Total contract value grew just 6%, raising concerns about the pace of new bookings and whether Palantir can sustain its rapid expansion. Combined with its premium valuation and the broader technology selloff, that has made the stock vulnerable despite its strong operating performance.

Palantir could also face new challenges in Washington following the Democrats’ victory in the midterm elections. With Democrats gaining control of Congress, President Trump’s proposed $1.5 trillion defense budget faces an uncertain future, potentially affecting Palantir’s ability to secure additional government contracts. The company could also come under greater scrutiny over its work with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), particularly as Democrats seek tighter oversight of federal surveillance and immigration enforcement.

Despite these concerns, Wall Street isn’t ready to give up on Palantir’s growth story. The stock carries a Moderate Buy consensus rating, based on 19 Buys, 5 Holds, and 2 Sells. Meanwhile, the average analyst price target of $229.09 implies about 33% upside from current levels. (See PLTR stock forecast)

data.title: Nvidia Stock Hit by 10 Downgrades — Here’s What Wall Street Analysts Have to Say
data.description:
There’s good news and bad news for Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) investors today, following the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang. The bad news is that Nvidia stock is falling nearly 5% on Thursday. The good news is that the selloff could have been much worse, given Huang’s immense influence over the chip giant’s success and his role in building its dominance in AI.

Still, Wall Street isn’t exactly brushing aside the leadership crisis, with Nvidia facing a wave of analyst downgrades over the past two days as concerns mount over what happens next.

Who Will Replace Jensen Huang?

Huang’s resignation followed revelations about his personal relationships, including an extramarital affair and allegations involving another senior Nvidia executive. While the circumstances surrounding his exit have received extensive coverage, investors now have another concern: who can take over a company so closely associated with its founder?

For now, CFO Colette Kress has stepped into the interim CEO position, providing some continuity while Nvidia’s board searches for a permanent replacement. Potential candidates include Ian Buck, the company’s vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, whose technical expertise could appeal to directors seeking an engineering-focused leader. Arm CEO Rene Haas has also been mentioned as a possible contender, given his previous experience at Nvidia and extensive semiconductor industry knowledge.

President Donald Trump has floated another possibility, suggesting former Apple CEO Tim Cook could be a suitable successor, although no formal candidacy has been announced.

10 Wall Street Analysts Downgrade Nvidia Stock

Wall Street wasted little time reacting to Huang’s departure, with ten analysts downgrading Nvidia and several making steep cuts to their price targets.

Truist analyst William Stein, who ranks 11th among more than 10,000 Wall Street analysts, downgraded Nvidia from Buy to Hold, while assigning a new price target of $174. Stein acknowledged that cutting his rating after the stock’s recent losses might seem poorly timed, but his concerns go well beyond Huang’s resignation. He warned that the leadership turmoil could damage Nvidia’s corporate culture, while the possibility that its GPUs reached Chinese companies and government entities raises additional risks for future revenue. With those uncertainties making earnings harder to forecast, Stein no longer believes a bullish recommendation is justified.

Bernstein’s Stacy Rasgon, who ranks among Wall Street’s top 2% of analysts, also downgraded Nvidia to Market Perform (i.e., Hold), cutting his price target in half from $400 to $200. Rasgon acknowledged the temptation to buy the dip but remains concerned that further revelations could complicate the company’s recovery. “We’ve had enough, and prefer to watch from the sidelines,” Rasgon commented.

Evercore ISI’s Mark Lipacis, ranked among the top 1% of analysts, downgraded NVDA to In Line (Hold), reducing his price target from $465 to $186. His concerns extend beyond succession, with expectations that Nvidia’s valuation multiple could continue contracting despite further upward earnings revisions.

KeyBanc’s John Vinh, who also ranks among the top 1% of Wall Street analysts, downgraded NVDA to Sector Weight (Hold), citing greater strategic and execution risks following Huang’s departure. Although he expects Nvidia’s underlying financial performance to remain resilient, Vinh believes finding someone with comparable leadership abilities will prove challenging.

William Blair’s Sebastien Naji joined the cautious camp, downgrading Nvidia to Market Perform (Hold) without assigning a price target. Naji believes the stock may have limited downside remaining, although governance concerns and uncertainty surrounding future operations warrant patience.

Completing the 10 downgrades, Melius Research’s Ben Reitzes moved to Hold, cutting his price target to $185 from $315, while Craig-Hallum’s Richard Shannon adopted the same neutral stance with a $180 target. Oppenheimer’s Rick Schafer downgraded Nvidia to Perform, withdrawing his previous price target amid concerns about retaining engineering talent following Huang’s departure.

StoneX analyst Cody Acree also downgraded Nvidia from Buy to Hold, suspending his previous $335 price target over concerns about the stock’s valuation following Huang’s departure, while leaving his earnings estimates unchanged. Meanwhile, Baird’s Tristan Gerra had downgraded NVDA to Neutral (Hold) on Wednesday, slashing his price target from $500 to $200 over leadership uncertainty, U.S. chip export restrictions on China, and potentially slower AI infrastructure spending growth.

What Does the Rest of Wall Street Think?

Despite 10 analysts stepping away from their bullish recommendations, the broader Street still sees upside potential for Nvidia. NVDA still maintains a Moderate Buy rating, based on 27 Buys, 10 Holds, and zero Sells. Meanwhile, the average 12-month price target of $257.10 suggests about 57% upside from current levels.
